notes.front: What does a differential backup store, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Files created or modified since the last full backup.
notes.explanation: A file changed after the last full backup is saved again by every differential backup until the next full backup.
notes.example: Like photocopying every page you have edited since the book's last full print run, each evening, until the next run.
notes.evidence: A differential backup stores files that were created or modified since the last full backup. Therefore, if a file is changed after the previous full backup, a differential backup will save the file each time until the next full backup is completed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 59

notes.front: What is a cold site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A facility with adequate space and infrastructure (power, telecommunications connections, environmental controls) to support system recovery activities.
notes.explanation: It supplies the space and utilities that recovery work needs.
notes.example: Like renting an empty unit with power and phone lines: you still have to bring the furniture.
notes.evidence: Cold Sites are typically facilities with adequate space and infrastructure (electric power, telecommunications connections, and environmental controls) to support information system recovery activities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: What is a warm site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A partially equipped office space containing some or all of the system hardware, software, telecommunications and power sources.
notes.explanation: Some or all of the systems may already be there, but the space is only partially equipped.
notes.example: Like a furnished holiday flat with some of your belongings already stored there, but not all.
notes.evidence: Warm Sites are partially equipped office spaces that contain some or all of the system hardware, software, telecommunications, and power sources.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: What is a hot site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A facility sized to support system requirements and configured with the necessary hardware, supporting infrastructure and support personnel.
notes.explanation: It includes support personnel as well as hardware and infrastructure.
notes.example: Like a second, fully staffed kitchen a restaurant chain keeps ready in case its main kitchen floods.
notes.evidence: Hot Sites are facilities appropriately sized to support system requirements and configured with the necessary system hardware, supporting infrastructure, and support personnel.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: What is a mobile site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A self-contained, transportable shell custom-fitted with the telecommunications and system equipment needed to meet system requirements.
notes.explanation: Being transportable, it can be brought to wherever it is needed.
notes.example: Like a mobile blood-donation lorry that brings the clinic to wherever it is needed.
notes.evidence: Mobile Sites are self-contained, transportable shells custom-fitted with specific telecommunications and system equipment necessary to meet system requirements.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: What is a mirrored site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A fully redundant facility with automated real-time information mirroring, identical to the primary site in all technical respects.
notes.explanation: It matches the primary site in every technical respect, with information mirrored automatically in real time.
notes.example: Like a stage show with an understudy who has rehearsed every line and stands in the wings each night.
notes.evidence: Mirrored Sites are fully redundant facilities with automated real-time information mirroring. Mirrored sites are identical to the primary site in all technical respects.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: How does SP 800-34's glossary define a reciprocal agreement?
notes.back: An agreement that allows two organisations to back up each other.
notes.explanation: Each organisation's site serves as the other's backup.
notes.example: Like two neighbouring schools agreeing that either may use the other's hall if its own is closed.
notes.evidence: Reciprocal Agreement: An agreement that allows two organizations to back up each other.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Appendix C Glossary, PDF p. 144

notes.front: What does a redundant array of independent disks (RAID) solution provide, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Disk redundancy.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 says disk redundancy can be provided by implementing RAID, and lists RAID among technologies to consider for a recovery strategy.
notes.example: Like writing your notes in two notebooks at once, so losing one notebook loses nothing.
notes.evidence: Disk redundancy can be provided for the direct access storage devices (DASDs) by implementing a RAID solution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.4.2 Mainframe Contingency Solutions, PDF p. 71

notes.front: What is high availability (HA), according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A process where redundancy and failover processes are built into a system to maximise its uptime and availability.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 sets the aim of HA at an uptime of 99.999 percent or higher.
notes.example: Like a hospital with a second generator that starts by itself the moment the mains power fails.
notes.evidence: HA is a process where redundancy and failover processes are built into a system to maximize its uptime and availability. The concept of HA is to achieve an uptime of 99.999 percent or higher
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.6 Use of High Availability (HA) Processes, PDF p. 62

notes.front: What are three factors, among others, that SP 800-53 says organisations consider when entering into alternate telecommunications agreements?
notes.back: Availability, quality of service (QoS) and access.
notes.explanation: Quality of service is one of the factors weighed alongside availability when choosing a backup telecommunications arrangement.
notes.example: Like comparing backup broadband providers on whether they can serve you, how good their service is, and whether you can get to it.
notes.evidence: Organizations consider factors such as availability, quality of service, and access when entering into alternate telecommunications agreements.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, CP-8 Telecommunications Services, PDF p. 151

notes.front: What kind of plan is a disaster recovery plan (DRP), and what does it restore, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: An information system-focused plan to restore operability of the target system, application or computer facility at an alternate site after an emergency.
notes.explanation: It is focused on the information system, restoring it at an alternate site rather than in place.
notes.example: Like a shop's plan for moving its tills and stock system into a temporary unit after a fire.
notes.evidence: A DRP is an information system-focused plan designed to restore operability of the target system, application, or computer facility infrastructure at an alternate site after an emergency.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 2.2.6 Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP), PDF p. 24

notes.front: In SP 800-34's sample plan, what does the outage assessment that follows notification determine?
notes.back: The extent of the disruption, any damage, and the expected recovery time.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 calls this step an outage assessment; this deck treats it as the damage assessment the exam names. Its results help the contingency plan coordinator run the recovery.
notes.example: Like a loss adjuster visiting after a burst pipe to see what is ruined and how long repairs will take.
notes.evidence: Following notification, a thorough outage assessment is necessary to determine the extent of the disruption, any damage, and expected recovery time. This outage assessment is conducted by {name of recovery team}. Assessment results are provided to the ISCP Coordinator to assist in the coordination of the recovery
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Appendix A.1 Sample Low-Impact ISCP, Section 3.3 Outage Assessment, PDF p. 79

notes.front: What happens during reconstitution, the third and final phase of SP 800-34's contingency plan?
notes.back: Recovery activities are completed, system capability is tested and validated, and normal system operations are resumed.
notes.explanation: It follows the activation and notification phase and the recovery phase.
notes.example: Like a theatre reopening after repairs: checking every light and seat before letting the audience back in.
notes.evidence: The Reconstitution Phase is the third and final phase of ISCP implementation and defines the actions taken to test and validate system capability and functionality. During Reconstitution, recovery activities are completed and normal system operations are resumed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.4 Reconstitution Phase, PDF p. 55

notes.front: What is a call tree, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: A manual notification method that assigns notification duties to specific people, who each notify other recovery personnel.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 calls it a common manual notification method.
notes.example: Like a school's snow-day phone chain, where each parent rings the next two families on the list.
notes.evidence: A common manual notification method is a call tree. This technique involves assigning notification duties to specific individuals, who in turn are responsible for notifying other recovery personnel.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures, PDF p. 51

notes.front: What is a test, training and exercise (TT&E) programme, according to SP 800-84?
notes.back: A programme through which an organisation carries out tests, training and exercises to keep its IT plans ready.
notes.explanation: SP 800-84 says organisations should consider having one because tests, training and exercises are so closely related.
notes.example: Like a fire service that runs drills, classroom lessons and hose-pressure checks under one yearly schedule.
notes.evidence: These three types of events can be carried out efficiently and effectively through the development and implementation of a test, training, and exercise (TT&E) program. Organizations should consider having such a program in place because tests, training, and exercises are so closely related.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 9

notes.front: In SP 800-84, which exercise has a facilitator present a scenario and question participants about roles, coordination and decisions, without deploying any equipment?
notes.back: A tabletop exercise.
notes.explanation: The scenario drives a discussion; nothing is actually deployed.
notes.example: Like a football manager talking the team through set pieces on a whiteboard, with no ball on the pitch.
notes.evidence: A facilitator presents a scenario and asks the exercise participants questions related to the scenario, which initiates a discussion among the participants of roles, responsibilities, coordination, and decision-making. A tabletop exercise is discussion-based only and does not involve deploying equipment or other resources.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: In SP 800-84, which exercise type lets personnel validate their operational readiness by performing their duties in a simulated operational environment?
notes.back: A functional exercise.
notes.explanation: It exercises the roles of specific team members, procedures and assets in one or more functional aspects of a plan.
notes.example: Like a lifeboat crew launching the boat on a calm day to rescue a dummy, rather than only discussing it.
notes.evidence: Functional exercises allow personnel to validate their operational readiness for emergencies by performing their duties in a simulated operational environment. Functional exercises are designed to exercise the roles and responsibilities of specific team members, procedures, and assets involved in one or more functional aspects of a plan
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: What does a full backup capture, and what is its main time drawback, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: All files on the disk or selected folder; the time needed to perform it can be lengthy.
notes.explanation: Because everything is on one media set, finding a particular file is simple.
notes.evidence: A full backup captures all files on the disk or within the folder selected for backup. Because all backed-up files are recorded to a single media or media set, locating a particular file or group of files is simple. However, the time required to perform a full backup can be lengthy.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 58

notes.front: What does an incremental backup capture, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Files created or changed since the last backup, regardless of backup type.
notes.explanation: Incremental backups use storage media more efficiently and take less time.
notes.evidence: An incremental backup captures files that were created or changed since the last backup, regardless of backup type. Incremental backups afford more efficient use of storage media, and backup times are reduced.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 58

notes.front: Why may restoring from a differential backup need fewer media than restoring from incremental backups, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Only the full backup media and the last differential media are needed.
notes.explanation: A differential backup also takes less time to complete than a full backup.
notes.evidence: A differential backup takes less time to complete than a full backup. Restoring from a differential backup may require fewer media than an incremental backup because only the full backup media and the last differential media would be needed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 59

notes.front: Why do differential backups take longer to complete than incremental backups, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: The amount of data since the last full backup grows each day until the next full backup.
notes.explanation: Each differential re-copies everything changed since the full backup, so its size keeps growing.
notes.evidence: As a disadvantage, differential backups take longer to complete than incremental backups because the amount of data since the last full backup increases each day until the next full backup is executed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 59

notes.front: Where does SP 800-34 say backup media should be stored?
notes.back: Offsite or at an alternate site, in a secure, environmentally controlled facility.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 gives this as a practice for client/server systems, repeating its earlier backup guidance.
notes.evidence: Store backups offsite or at an alternate site. As mentioned in Section 3.4.2, backup media should be stored offsite or at an alternate site in a secure, environmentally controlled facility.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.2.2 Client/Server Systems Contingency Solutions, PDF p. 63

notes.front: What are two recovery arrangements SP 800-34 says a system recovery strategy may include?
notes.back: Any two of: commercial contracts with alternate site vendors, reciprocal agreements with internal or external organisations, service-level agreements with equipment vendors.
notes.explanation: These are the specific recovery methods SP 800-34 says should be considered when building a strategy.
notes.evidence: Specific recovery methods further described in Section 3.4.2 should be considered and may include commercial contracts with alternate site vendors, reciprocal agreements with internal or external organizations, and service-level agreements (SLAs) with equipment vendors.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.1 Backup and Recovery, PDF p. 34

notes.front: Which alternate site option does SP 800-34 call the most expensive, and what does it ensure?
notes.back: The mirrored site; it ensures virtually 100 percent availability.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 notes obvious cost and ready-time differences among the site options.
notes.evidence: There are obvious cost and ready-time differences among the options. In these examples, the mirrored site is the most expensive choice, but it ensures virtually 100 percent availability.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: What is the trade-off of a cold site, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: It is the least expensive to maintain, but may need substantial time to acquire and install equipment.
notes.explanation: Partially equipped sites, such as warm sites, fall in the middle of the spectrum.
notes.evidence: Cold sites are the least expensive to maintain, although they may require substantial time to acquire and install necessary equipment. Partially equipped sites, such as warm sites, fall in the middle of the spectrum.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: Why does SP 800-34 say a reciprocal agreement should be entered into carefully?
notes.back: Each site must be able to support the other, in addition to its own workload, in a disaster.
notes.explanation: The two organisations must also prioritise the recovery sequence of both organisations' systems jointly.
notes.evidence: A reciprocal agreement should be entered into carefully because each site must be able to support the other, in addition to its own workload, in the event of a disaster. This type of agreement requires the recovery sequence for the systems from both organizations to be prioritized from a joint perspective, favorable to both parties.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 37

notes.front: What risk does SP 800-34 warn about when contracting a commercial alternate site?
notes.back: Several organisations may contract for the same site, so it may not accommodate all of them if a disaster hits many at once.
notes.explanation: The risk arises when one disaster affects enough of the vendor's customers at the same time.
notes.evidence: Customers should be aware that multiple organizations may contract with a vendor for the same alternate site; as a result, the site may be unable to accommodate all of the customers if a disaster affects enough of those customers simultaneously.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 37

notes.front: How do redundancy and fault tolerance methods protect stored data, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: They store data on more than one drive, eliminating data loss from single drive failures.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 presents them as methods for maintaining the integrity of stored data.
notes.evidence: There are several methods available to maintain the integrity of stored data. These methods use redundancy and fault tolerance processes to store data on more than one drive and eliminate loss of data from single drive failures.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 58

notes.front: How much downtime a year does SP 800-34 equate with the high availability goal of 99.999 percent uptime?
notes.back: Just a few minutes per year.
notes.explanation: Five nines is the uptime target SP 800-34 sets for HA.
notes.evidence: The concept of HA is to achieve an uptime of 99.999 percent or higher, which equates to just a few minutes per year of downtime.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.6 Use of High Availability (HA) Processes, PDF p. 62

notes.front: For which systems does SP 800-34 say high availability should be considered, and why only those?
notes.back: Only systems that cannot tolerate downtime, such as air traffic or financial systems, because HA is expensive.
notes.explanation: HA systems normally carry higher maintenance and support costs, so HA is not viable for many systems.
notes.evidence: Normally, there are higher cost maintenance and support requirements associated with HA systems. Therefore, HA is not a viable option for many systems and should be considered only for those systems that cannot tolerate downtime. Examples of this may be air traffic systems and financial systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.6 Use of High Availability (HA) Processes, PDF p. 62

notes.front: Why can high availability not replace a solid backup strategy, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Data corruption may propagate through the HA system, and without a separate backup, recovery may not be possible.
notes.explanation: Redundancy copies bad data as faithfully as good data.
notes.evidence: Also, HA systems cannot be a replacement for a solid backup strategy, as a corruption of data on a system may propagate through an HA system, making the system unusable. Without a backup of the system separate from the system itself, recovery may not be possible.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.6 Use of High Availability (HA) Processes, PDF p. 62

notes.front: Which information system disruptions does a DRP address, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: Only those that require relocation.
notes.explanation: Once the alternate facility is set up, individual contingency plans may handle recovery of each affected system.
notes.evidence: The DRP may be supported by multiple information system contingency plans to address recovery of impacted individual systems once the alternate facility has been established. A DRP may support a BCP or COOP plan by recovering supporting systems for mission/business processes or mission essential functions at an alternate location. The DRP only addresses information system disruptions that require relocation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 2.2.6 Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP), PDF p. 24

notes.front: SP 800-34's contingency plan recovery is implemented in three phases: activation and notification, {{c1::recovery}}, and reconstitution.
notes.explanation: The phases run in that order, ending with reconstitution.
notes.evidence: The ISCP recovery is implemented in three phases: (1) Activation and Notification, (2) Recovery, and (3) Reconstitution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.1 Supporting Information, PDF p. 49

notes.front: What three activities does SP 800-34's activation and notification phase include?
notes.back: Notifying recovery personnel, conducting an outage assessment, and activating the plan.
notes.explanation: The phase covers the first actions once a disruption has been detected or appears imminent.
notes.evidence: The Activation and Notification Phase defines initial actions taken once a system disruption or outage has been detected or appears to be imminent. This phase includes activities to notify recovery personnel, conduct an outage assessment, and activate the plan.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.2 Activation and Notification Phase, PDF p. 50

notes.front: What are the two major activities of SP 800-34's reconstitution phase?
notes.back: Validating successful recovery, and deactivating the plan.
notes.explanation: Validating recovery and deactivating the plan together close out the contingency effort.
notes.evidence: This phase consists of two major activities: validating successful recovery and deactivation of the plan.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.4 Reconstitution Phase, PDF p. 55

notes.front: In SP 800-34's reconstitution phase, what is concurrent processing?
notes.back: Running a system at two separate locations at once until there is assurance the recovered system operates correctly and securely.
notes.explanation: It is one of the validation steps before normal operations resume.
notes.evidence: Concurrent processing is the process of running a system at two separate locations concurrently until there is a level of assurance that the recovered system is operating correctly and securely.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.4 Reconstitution Phase, PDF p. 55

notes.front: Before the contingency plan is deactivated, what document does SP 800-34 say should record lessons learned?
notes.back: An after-action report, used to update the contingency plan.
notes.explanation: All recovery and reconstitution events, including actions and problems, should be well documented first.
notes.evidence: All recovery and reconstitution events should be well documented, including actions taken and problems encountered during the recovery and reconstitution efforts. An after-action report with lessons learned should be documented and included for updating the ISCP.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.4 Reconstitution Phase, PDF p. 56

notes.front: For high-impact systems, what should SP 800-34's full-scale functional exercise include?
notes.back: A system failover to the alternate location.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 says the full-scale functional exercise should be run at an organisation-defined frequency.
notes.evidence: For high-impact systems, a full-scale functional exercise at an organization-defined frequency should be conducted. The full-scale functional exercise should include a system failover to the alternate location.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.5.4 Exercises, PDF p. 44

notes.front: When does SP 800-84 say organisations should conduct TT&E events?
notes.back: Periodically; after organisational changes, IT plan updates or new TT&E guidance; or as otherwise needed.
notes.explanation: This helps keep plans reasonable, effective and complete, and ensures personnel know their roles.
notes.evidence: Organizations should conduct TT&E events periodically; following organizational changes, updates to an IT plan, or the issuance of new TT&E guidance; or as otherwise needed. This assists organizations in ensuring that their IT plans are reasonable, effective, and complete, and that all personnel know what their roles are in the conduct of each IT plan.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: After a suspected key compromise affecting sensitive or critical information, what does SP 800-57 Part 1 say should be conducted?
notes.back: An immediate damage assessment.
notes.explanation: SP 800-57 ties the immediate assessment to cases where sensitive or critical information or processes are affected.
notes.evidence: where sensitive or critical information or processes are affected, an immediate damage assessment should be conducted.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Recommendation for Key Management, Section 6.1 Compromise recovery, PDF p. 137

notes.front: A server gets a full backup on Sunday and a backup every weeknight. After Thursday's failure, the team needs only Sunday's media and Wednesday night's. Which nightly backup type is in use?
notes.back: Differential.
notes.choices:
A) Incremental
B) Differential
C) Full
notes.choicesExplained: A: restoring incrementals needs the full backup plus every night's incremental media. C: nightly full backups would need only Wednesday's media, not Sunday's.
notes.explanation: Only the full backup and the last differential are needed to restore from differential backups.
notes.evidence: Restoring from a differential backup may require fewer media than an incremental backup because only the full backup media and the last differential media would be needed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 59

notes.front: A clinic keeps its backup tapes on a shelf in the same room as the server. What does SP 800-34 advise?
notes.back: Store them offsite or at an alternate site, in a secure, environmentally controlled facility.
notes.choices:
A) Lock the room
B) Store them offsite or at an alternate site, in a secure, environmentally controlled facility
C) Keep them in a desk drawer at a manager's home
notes.choicesExplained: A: locking the room leaves the tapes on the same site as the server. C: a home drawer is offsite but not a secure, environmentally controlled facility.
notes.explanation: A shelf beside the server is neither offsite nor at an alternate site.
notes.evidence: backup media should be stored offsite or at an alternate site in a secure, environmentally controlled facility.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.2.2 Client/Server Systems Contingency Solutions, PDF p. 63

notes.front: A small charity can tolerate its systems being down for weeks and has a tight budget. Which alternate site type best fits?
notes.back: A cold site.
notes.choices:
A) A cold site
B) A hot site
C) A mirrored site
notes.choicesExplained: B: a hot site costs more to keep ready than the charity needs. C: a mirrored site is the most expensive option of all.
notes.explanation: Cold sites are the cheapest to maintain; their long setup time matters less when weeks of downtime are acceptable.
notes.evidence: Cold sites are the least expensive to maintain, although they may require substantial time to acquire and install necessary equipment.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: An emergency-dispatch service must be back in operation within hours of losing its data centre, with staff and equipment ready. Which alternate site type fits?
notes.back: A hot site.
notes.choices:
A) A cold site
B) A warm site
C) A hot site
notes.choicesExplained: A: a cold site has space and power but equipment must still be acquired and installed. B: a warm site is only partially equipped.
notes.explanation: Only a hot site comes configured with the hardware, supporting infrastructure and support personnel already in place.
notes.evidence: Hot Sites are facilities appropriately sized to support system requirements and configured with the necessary system hardware, supporting infrastructure, and support personnel.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: A firm rents a standby office that already holds some of its servers and phone lines; it would need to add the rest before going live. What kind of site is this?
notes.back: A warm site.
notes.choices:
A) A cold site
B) A warm site
C) A mirrored site
notes.choicesExplained: A: a cold site has space and infrastructure but not the systems. C: a mirrored site is identical to the primary site and mirrors data in real time.
notes.explanation: Some but not all of the system hardware and telecommunications are in place, which is what SP 800-34 calls a warm site.
notes.evidence: Warm Sites are partially equipped office spaces that contain some or all of the system hardware, software, telecommunications, and power sources.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 36

notes.front: Two county councils with identical systems agree to host each other's systems after a disaster. What must each check before signing, according to SP 800-34?
notes.back: That its site can carry the other's workload as well as its own.
notes.choices:
A) That the other council uses the same insurer
B) That its site can carry the other's workload as well as its own
C) That the sites are at least 24 hours apart by road
notes.choicesExplained: A: SP 800-34 does not make insurance the test. C: SP 800-34 sets no such distance rule for reciprocal sites.
notes.explanation: A reciprocal agreement only works if each site can support the other on top of its own load.
notes.evidence: A reciprocal agreement should be entered into carefully because each site must be able to support the other, in addition to its own workload, in the event of a disaster.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, PDF p. 37

notes.front: One disk in a file server fails, yet no data is lost and users notice nothing. Which technology most likely made the difference?
notes.back: A redundant array of independent disks.
notes.choices:
A) A redundant array of independent disks
B) A differential backup
C) A cold site
notes.choicesExplained: B: a backup allows data to be restored afterwards, but users would notice the outage. C: a cold site is an alternate facility, not protection against one disk failing.
notes.explanation: RAID provides disk redundancy, which a backup or an alternate site does not.
notes.evidence: Disk redundancy can be provided for the direct access storage devices (DASDs) by implementing a RAID solution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.4.2 Mainframe Contingency Solutions, PDF p. 71

notes.front: A bank's payments system now runs as a high availability cluster, and a manager proposes ending separate backups. What does SP 800-34 say?
notes.back: Keep backups: corrupted data can propagate through the HA system, and recovery may be impossible without them.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: HA makes backups redundant
B) Keep backups: corrupted data can propagate through the HA system, and recovery may be impossible without them
C) Keep backups only for the next year
notes.choicesExplained: A: HA cannot replace a solid backup strategy. C: the risk of corruption spreading through the HA system does not end after a year.
notes.explanation: HA protects against component failure, not against bad data being copied everywhere.
notes.evidence: HA systems cannot be a replacement for a solid backup strategy, as a corruption of data on a system may propagate through an HA system, making the system unusable.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.6 Use of High Availability (HA) Processes, PDF p. 62

notes.front: A flood makes a head office unusable for months, and its systems must be moved to a temporary site. Which plan in SP 800-34 is designed for this?
notes.back: The disaster recovery plan.
notes.choices:
A) The occupant emergency plan
B) The disaster recovery plan
C) A call tree
notes.choicesExplained: A: the occupant emergency plan protects people during an incident, not systems. C: a call tree only notifies recovery staff.
notes.explanation: The DRP restores the target system or facility infrastructure at an alternate site after an emergency.
notes.evidence: A DRP is an information system-focused plan designed to restore operability of the target system, application, or computer facility infrastructure at an alternate site after an emergency.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 2.2.6 Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP), PDF p. 24

notes.front: A power surge knocks out a data centre. Recovery staff have been called. According to SP 800-34, what should they do before choosing how to run the recovery?
notes.back: Assess the outage: its cause, the extent of disruption and damage, and expected recovery time.
notes.choices:
A) Start reconstitution straight away
B) Assess the outage: its cause, the extent of disruption and damage, and expected recovery time
C) Deactivate the plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: reconstitution is the final phase, after recovery. C: the plan is deactivated only when reconstitution is complete.
notes.explanation: The assessment of the nature and extent of the disruption decides how the contingency plan is implemented.
notes.evidence: To determine how the ISCP will be implemented following a system disruption or outage, it is essential to assess the nature and extent of the disruption.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.2.3 Outage Assessment, PDF p. 52

notes.front: Systems are running again at the alternate site. The team now checks that restored databases are complete and current to the last backup before declaring normal operations. Which phase is this?
notes.back: Reconstitution.
notes.choices:
A) Activation and notification
B) Recovery
C) Reconstitution
notes.choicesExplained: A: activation and notification is about notifying staff, assessing the outage and activating the plan. B: recovery restores capabilities; validating them before normal operations belongs to reconstitution.
notes.explanation: Validating recovery, including data testing, is one of the reconstitution phase's two major activities.
notes.evidence: Validation Data Testing. Data testing is the process of testing and validating recovered data to ensure that data files or databases have been recovered completely and are current to the last available backup.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 4.4 Reconstitution Phase, PDF p. 55

notes.front: A team times whether its whole call cascade completes within 20 minutes. Under SP 800-84, which kind of TT&E event is this?
notes.back: A test.
notes.choices:
A) A test
B) Training
C) A tabletop exercise
notes.choicesExplained: B: training informs staff of their roles and teaches skills. C: a tabletop exercise is discussion only, with nothing measured in operation.
notes.explanation: It uses a quantifiable measure to validate operability, which is how SP 800-84 describes tests.
notes.evidence: Tests are evaluation tools that use quantifiable metrics to validate the operability of an IT system or system component in an operational environment specified in an IT plan.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 9

notes.front: Department heads sit round a table while a facilitator describes a ransomware scenario and asks who would decide what. No systems are touched. What is this?
notes.back: A tabletop exercise.
notes.choices:
A) A tabletop exercise
B) A functional exercise
C) A test
notes.choicesExplained: B: in a functional exercise staff perform their duties in a simulated environment. C: a test measures operability with quantifiable metrics.
notes.explanation: It is discussion-based only and deploys no equipment or other resources.
notes.evidence: Tabletop exercises are discussion-based exercises where personnel meet in a classroom setting or in breakout groups to discuss their roles during an emergency and their responses to a particular emergency situation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: The recovery team actually restores servers from backup and sends emergency notifications in a simulated environment, as it would in a real outage. What is this?
notes.back: A functional exercise.
notes.choices:
A) A tabletop exercise
B) A functional exercise
C) Training
notes.choicesExplained: A: a tabletop exercise is discussion-based only. C: training informs staff of roles and teaches skills rather than performing them in a simulated emergency.
notes.explanation: Staff perform their duties in a simulated operational environment, which is what a functional exercise involves.
notes.evidence: Functional exercises allow staff to execute their roles and responsibilities as they would in an actual emergency situation, but in a simulated manner.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Using SP 800-34's sample site criteria, how does a cold site compare with a hot site on cost, hardware and setup time?
notes.back: Cold: low cost, no hardware, long setup. Hot: medium to high cost, full hardware, short setup.
notes.explanation: Warm sites sit in the middle on every one of these criteria.
notes.evidence: Site Cost Cold Site Warm Site Hot Site Low Medium Medium/High Hardware Equipment None Partial Full Telecommunications Setup Time Location None Partial/Full Full Long Medium Short
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 3.4.3 Alternate Sites, Table 3-3 Sample Alternate Site Criteria, PDF p. 37

notes.front: What is the difference in reference point between an incremental and a differential backup?
notes.back: Incremental: changes since the last backup of any type. Differential: changes since the last full backup.
notes.explanation: SP 800-34 defines the differential backup, by contrast, as storing files changed since the last full backup.
notes.evidence: An incremental backup captures files that were created or changed since the last backup, regardless of backup type.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, Section 5.1.2 Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup, PDF p. 58

notes.front: In SP 800-84, what separates a tabletop exercise from a functional exercise?
notes.back: A tabletop is discussion only; a functional exercise has staff perform their duties in a simulated operational environment.
notes.explanation: Both validate a plan, but only the functional exercise has people carrying out their duties.
notes.evidence: A tabletop exercise is discussion-based only and does not involve deploying equipment or other resources. – Functional Exercises. Functional exercises allow personnel to validate their operational readiness for emergencies by performing their duties in a simulated operational environment.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10
